extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional screenwriters, dramatists, and storytellers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance for designing and composing screen stories: choosing material, structuring events/scenes/sequences, establishing stakes (values), and using beats and conflict to create turning moments that engage an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Story
rubrics_metrics.description: “A good story makes a good film possible...failure to make the story work virtually guarantees disaster.” The story is primary; dialogue and description are subordinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize story design over polishing dialogue or description. Beautiful images or sharp dialogue cannot save a story that lacks progression, motivation, or meaningful subtext. If you can't tell story, literary flourishes waste the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Story-Design Questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the total creative effort...75 percent or more of a writer’s labor goes into designing story. Who are these characters? What do they want? Why do they want it? How do they go about getting it? What stops them? What are the consequences?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat answering these six questions as the central design task. Shape your narrative decisions (events, scenes, character actions) around clear answers to these questions; they determine motivation, obstacles, and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Story: material worth telling
rubrics_metrics.description: “Good story” means something worth telling that the world wants to hear. Finding this begins with talent, vision, fresh insights into human nature and society, and in-depth knowledge of characters and world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose material that expresses ‘Big-T’ Truth (deeper meaning) rather than mere factual reportage. Combine instinct/talent with a strong, personal vision and empathy for characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'Loves' that Drive a Storyteller
rubrics_metrics.description: A storyteller must have the love of story, the dramatic, truth, humanity, sensation, dreaming, humor, language, duality, perfection, uniqueness, beauty, and self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate these sensibilities—they fuel judgment, perseverance, willingness to revise, and the capacity to empathize and imagine. The list is a checklist of artist-attitudes needed to seek and sustain strong stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of Craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft is the sum total of all means used to draw the audience into deep involvement, to hold that involvement, and ultimately to reward it with a moving and meaningful experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop technique deliberately: write, step out, read, analyze—ask 'Is it good? Why not? Cut? Add? Reorder?' Rewriting guided by craft frees the subconscious and refines instinct. Craft is not gimmickry but the concert of techniques that enable meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Portraiture (Personal-Story Anti-Pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'personal story' bad script is understructured, slice-of-life portraiture that mistakes verisimilitude for truth—fact is not the same as Big-T Truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't confuse meticulous factual observation with meaningful story. Abstract from life to reveal deeper truths; if a script is merely reportage of events with no underlying truth or structure, it will feel banal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Spectacle (Commercial-Success Anti-Pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'guaranteed commercial success' bad script is an overstructured, overcomplicated assault on the senses that bears no relationship to life—kinesis or effects are not a substitute for story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle (CGI, chases, effects) must be motivated by and subordinate to story. If effects call attention to themselves rather than enriching the story, entertainment is short-lived. Use technical innovation only to serve human truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as Metaphor for Life
rubrics_metrics.description: A storyteller is a life poet who transforms day-to-day living, inner life and outer life, dream and actuality into a poem whose rhyme scheme is events rather than words—a two-hour metaphor that says: Life is like this!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract from life to find essences and meanings; avoid pure verbatim realism or empty abstraction. The story must both resonate with life-as-lived and reveal a deeper observation about it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Sensory Perception and Imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: At one end of reality is pure fact; at the other, pure imagination. Strong storytelling strikes a balance along this spectrum—sensitive sensory perception complemented by a lively imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop both powers: the ability to render vivid, observable detail and the ability to imagine beyond the given. Too much on either pole weakens story; integrate both to produce meaningful fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Talent vs Literary Talent
rubrics_metrics.description: The material of literary talent is words; the material of story talent is life itself. Literary talent (verbal craft) is common; story talent (shaping life into telling) is rare—and story talent is primary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize developing story talent (structure, event selection, conflict) while using literary skills to enhance expression. Talent without craft is like fuel without an engine—learn craft to channel talent productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: selection of events with a purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: STRUCTURE is a selection of events from the characters’ life stories that is composed into a strategic sequence to arouse specific emotions and to express a specific view of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select which moments to show and which to leave out with the purpose of arousing particular emotional responses and communicating an idea about life. Know your purpose before composing events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Event: value + conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: A STORY EVENT creates meaningful change in the life situation of a character that is expressed and experienced in terms of a VALUE and ACHIEVED THROUGH CONFLICT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events must affect characters and be meaningful (not trivial); they must bear a value at stake (e.g., love/hatred, life/death) and the change must arise through motivated conflict rather than mere coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Values: binary stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: STORY VALUES are the universal qualities of human experience that may shift from positive to negative, or negative to positive, from one moment to the next (e.g., alive/dead, love/hate, hope/despair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the value at stake in every event/scene. Use clear, charged oppositions as the currency of stakes so the audience can experience changes emotionally and intellectually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene as Story Event (the 'Turn' test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A SCENE is an action through conflict in more or less continuous time and space that turns the value-charged condition of a character’s life on at least one value with a degree of perceptible significance. Ideally, every scene is a STORY EVENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test each scene by asking: What value is at stake at the opening? Where is it at the close? If the value is unchanged, the scene is likely a nonevent (often pure exposition) and should be cut or reworked so it turns. No scene that doesn’t turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition is not a scene justification
rubrics_metrics.description: If exposition is a scene’s sole justification, a disciplined writer will trash it and weave its information into the film elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid isolated expository scenes. Integrate necessary background and information into scenes that also change value or advance conflict, or reframe the material so it becomes part of an event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats: units of action/reaction inside scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: A BEAT is an exchange of behavior in action/reaction. Beat by beat these changing behaviors shape the turning of a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break scenes into beats—distinct behaviors or exchanges that alter the scene’s emotional charge. Build momentum beat-by-beat toward the scene’s Turning Point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence: linked scenes culminating in greater change
rubrics_metrics.description: A SEQUENCE is a series of scenes—generally two to five—that culminates with greater impact than any previous scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange scenes into sequences that escalate stakes and lead to a determinant capping scene. Use sequences to structure mid-level dramatic movement between beats/scenes and the larger acts of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene Unity vs Camera Setups
rubrics_metrics.description: The four shifts of place—bedroom to kitchen to garage to highway—are camera setups but not true scenes if the value doesn’t change until the Turning Point. Generally the test is: could it have been written 'in one' (unity of time and place)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between cinematic setups and actual scene-events. A scene may span locations for cinematic reasons, but its status as a scene depends on whether it contains a value turn; the Turning Point defines the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical Scene Count
rubrics_metrics.description: For a typical film, the writer will choose forty to sixty Story Events or, as they’re commonly known, scenes. A novelist may want more than sixty, a playwright rarely as many as forty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these typical ranges as planning guidance for pacing and structural scope. Adjust according to medium and story needs, but design with an awareness of scene economy.
